stories.headline: Drug war is everyone’s fight: DGP Prabhat
stories.title: Drug war is everyone’s fight: DGP Prabhat
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 12: Director General of Police (DGP) Nalin Prabhat on Monday called for a united societal response to the growing challenge of drug abuse, asserting that protecting children and young people from narcotics was a collective responsibility that extended far beyond the police force. Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of a function at Police Public School here, the DGP said the campaign against drugs was gaining momentum across Jammu and Kashmir under the leadership of Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha. He said the future of the country depended on safeguarding its younger generation from substance abuse. “These small children are the future of our country,” Prabhat said, underlining the need for society to come together to protect young people from the menace. Referring to recent enforcement action against drug trafficking in Srinagar, the J&K Police chief said several arrests had been made as part of the crackdown. He emphasised that tackling the problem required a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach, with active participation from citizens. “It is our duty that we participate in this fight and say no to drugs,” he said, urging people to join the campaign against narcotics. The DGP's appeal comes as Jammu & Kashmir Police intensifies efforts to raise awareness about drug abuse alongside enforcement action against traffickers. The emphasis on community participation places families, educational institutions and local communities at the centre of efforts to prevent substance abuse and protect vulnerable youth. As part of the awareness drive, the DGP flagged off a motorcycle rally from Police Public School, Bemina, Srinagar, towards Ekta Nagar in Gujarat for the Rashtriya Ekta Diwas parade scheduled for October 31. The contingent comprises 10 bikers from Jammu and Kashmir Police and five from Ladakh Police. Awareness programmes on the harmful effects of drug abuse are planned along the route, with a focus on sensitising young people and promoting the message of a drug-free society. The initiative combines public outreach with the broader campaign against narcotics, seeking to carry the message beyond police establishments and into communities. The DGP’s message was clear-- enforcement against traffickers must go hand in hand with public awareness, prevention and collective responsibility if Jammu and Kashmir is to protect its next generation from the consequences of drug abuse.

In 1993, Jantar Mantar emerged as the capital's new square for dissent.
Nearly 33 years later, the BJP-led Centre has redrawn Delhi's protest map.

The lawns near India Gate, Parliament and the government's administrative nerve centre began to be viewed as a security and crowd-control challenge.

article_sentences: The by-election results in West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, declared on Friday, held few surprises.
Barely five months after the April Assembly elections, the ruling party in each State/UT won all five bypolls.
What varied was the scale of victory.
In West Bengal, the BJP retained Nandigram and wrested Rejinagar, with strong vote shares of 76% and 63%.
In Puducherry, the ruling.
All India N.R. Congress also registered an emphatic win — 61% of the votes — in Thattanchavady.
Nandigram and Thattanchavady were vacated by the Chief Ministers, which partly explains the strong wins.
But the contests in Tamil Nadu were closer.
Dharapuram and Madurantakam fell vacant after their AIADMK MLAs resigned and defected to the ruling TVK, which renominated them.
Both won their seats back with 37% and 40% of the vote, respectively, leading the DMK rival candidates by about eight percentage points.
By-elections tend to favour the party in power, as voters prefer representatives with access to government.
But the variance between West Bengal and Tamil Nadu reflects the nature of contest in two similarly sized States but with vastly different political cultures.

stories.headline: Karnataka High Court Directs Police To Secure LOC Against Husband In Dowry Case
stories.title: Karnataka High Court Directs Police To Secure LOC Against Husband In Dowry Case
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Karnataka High Court on Monday [October 12] directed the police to take steps for the issuance of the Look Out Circular (LOC) against the husband of a woman who has accused him of cruelty and dowry harassment, while ordering hand delivery of the order.

The single judge bench of Justice Anant Ramananth Hegde passed the interim direction while hearing a criminal petition filed by the wife seeking a direction to the police to issue LOC against her husband- a working professional at France.
The direction is subject to Court's final order.

The wife has contended that her husband remains in India only for the reissuance of his supposedly lost passport, and that his departure afterwards would irretrievably damage her cause and further investigation in the FIR.
The Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) had in October rejected her application under Section 175(3) r/w Section 94 of the BNSS for the same reliefs.

Yesterday, when the matter was taken up, Advocate Angad Kamath, appearing for the petitioner, submitted that not intimating the respondent husband about the issuance of the LOC would not infringe upon his rights under the Constitution of India, and that the LOC can be issued subject to the guidelines issued therein.

“…It is well settled that mere inability to pay the money without there being a criminal case cannot be a reason to take away the fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution of India…”.

Kamath submitted that while dowry harassment is part of the allegations, the purported inability to pay money by the accused, as mentioned by the magistrate in the order, had nothing to do with the case or the issuance of the LOC sought for.
He pointed out that there are two named accused, the mother-in-law and the husband.
The husband is a resident of France, and once he goes back, he cannot be secured for investigation.
Though he is a passport holder of India, he has been a resident of France for 3 years, Kamath added.
He holds a visa of Tunisia and France, and all he requires is a boarding pass to leave the country forever, it was submitted further.

stories.title: Say no to drugs, protect future: DGP Nalin Prabhat
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 12: Director General of Police Nalin Prabhat on Monday called for a whole-of-society approach in the fight against drug abuse, even as he flagged off a National Motorcycle Rally carrying the message of a Nasha Mukt society. Speaking to mediapersons on the sidelines of the programme here at Police Public School, the DGP said the anti-drug campaign was being pursued across the country and had gained considerable momentum in Jammu and Kashmir under the leadership of Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha. Referring to recent enforcement action in the summer capital Srinagar, he said that several people had been arrested as part of the ongoing crackdown. “These small children are the future of our country,” Prabhat told reporters, stressing that protecting the younger generation from substance abuse was a shared responsibility. He described the campaign as a collective fight that required more than law enforcement action alone. “This is a war being fought across society, with a whole-of-government approach. It is our duty that we participate in this fight and say no to drugs,” he said. The DGP said this after flagging off the motorcycle rally comprising 10 bikers of the Jammu and Kashmir Police and five from the Ladakh Police. The contingent is headed for Ekta Nagar in Gujarat and will form part of the nationwide contingents converging for the Rashtriya Ekta Diwas Parade on October 31, 2026, to mark the birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. The theme of the rally is “Fight Against Drugs,” and the participants will conduct awareness programmes en route to sensitise people, particularly the youth. Prior to the flag-off, an awareness programme on the fight against drugs was held at the school, drawing enthusiastic participation from a large number of students. Senior officers present included Special DG Coordination S.J.M. Gillani, Additional DG Armed Nitish Kumar, IGP Headquarters Bhim Sen Tuti, IGP Kashmir Sujit Kumar and DIG Armed Range Kashmir Maqsood-ul-Zaman, the nodal officer for the J&K Police contingent. Nalin Prabhat expressed satisfaction over the initiatives being undertaken to realise the vision of the Prime Minister and the Lieutenant Governor towards building a drug-free society. He also appreciated the participation of the J&K Police in the national motorcycle rally, in which 45 contingents from states, Union Territories and Central Armed Police Forces are taking part.

stories.headline: Saudis probe how defence systems failed to stop deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh airport
stories.title: Saudis probe how defence systems failed to stop deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh airport
stories.summary: Cairo, Oct 13: Saudi Arabia has launched an investigation to determine how its air defences failed to intercept a barrage of missiles and drones fired by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, including an attack on Riyadh airport that killed at least 13 people and wounded over 300, two regional officials said Monday. The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly, said the initial probe showed that Yemen's Houthis first fired multiple drones to pave the way for a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles to reach Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport. The Houthis possess ballistic missiles and advanced systems fitted with warheads that can change direction during flight and pose a challenge to Patriot interceptors and other defence systems used by the Saudis. One of the officials said the investigation also aims to find out why air defence systems did not provide earlier warning of the attack in which the Houthi missiles and drones flew over 1,000 kilometres (620 miles) to reach Riyadh. The incident, one of a string of Houthi attacks since last week on Saudi airports, has exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi Arabia's defence system and signalled a dangerous inflexion point in an expanding Middle East conflict that began more than seven months ago when the US and Israel launched their war against Iran. The Saudi-led coalition also said it had twice intercepted and destroyed ballistic missiles launched Monday by Yemen's Houthi rebels toward Riyadh. At least three explosions could be heard Monday night in the city. There was no immediate claim of responsibility. Civil Defence officials later said the danger had passed. stories.headline: Russian diesel for America: The double standards in Trump’s energy policy needs an answer
stories.title: Russian diesel for America: The double standards in Trump’s energy policy needs an answer
stories.summary: New Delhi, October 12: Trump’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian fuel exposes the gap between Washington’s energy needs and its demands on others. India must defend its right to make independent choices based on national interest. US President Donald Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel into American markets has raised an important question about the consistency of Washington’s policy towards Moscow. For years, the United States has pressured India to reduce/stop its purchases of Russian oil, arguing that the revenue helps finance Russia’s war against Ukraine. Now, when rising fuel prices threaten American consumers and the Republican Party’s prospects in the November midterm elections, Trump himself has turned to Russia for supplies. The visible difference is clear. When India buys Russian oil, the US raises objections. But when America needs Russian diesel, it finds a way to make the deal happen. This raises questions about fairness and whether every country has the right to take decisions based on its own needs without facing political pressure. America puts its own interests first. Trump has announced a deal under which Russia will supply diesel to the US and other markets in the coming months. To make this possible, his administration has temporarily relaxed sanctions on Russian diesel exports. The immediate reason is clear. The war involving the United States, Israel and Iran has disrupted energy supplies, particularly through the Strait of Hormuz. Diesel prices in America have risen sharply, affecting farmers, truckers, businesses and ordinary households. With elections approaching, the administration is under pressure to bring down costs. There is nothing unusual about a government protecting its own economic interests. Every country is expected to do so. The problem arises when Washington expects other countries to follow one set of rules while keeping the freedom to change its own approach when circumstances demand it. If buying Russian fuel can be justified by American economic needs, India’s energy requirements deserve the same consideration. India cannot compromise its energy security India is one of the world’s largest energy consumers and depends heavily on imported crude oil. Its energy choices affect transport costs, inflation, agriculture, industry and the household budgets of millions of people. Russian crude oil became an important source for India and several allies after the Ukraine conflict because it was available at discounted prices. For India, buying Russian oil is not only a practical economic decision based on price, availability, and energy security, but also a decision made by a dependent ally, and in no way should it be seen as an endorsement of Moscow’s policies. India, time and again, has made it clear to the US and others that its energy decisions are guided by national interest. While the US can impose its own sanctions, it cannot dictate India’s energy choices. India should now be strong enough to stand firm against any attempt to turn oil purchases into a test of political loyalty. Trump’s latest move makes Washington’s earlier pressure on India more difficult to defend politically. If Russian oil revenues are the central concern, then American purchases of Russian diesel raise the same question: will the money earned by Moscow not also strengthen its economy? The argument is not that India and the United States face identical circumstances or that crude oil and refined diesel are exactly the same product. The legal arrangements may also differ. But the underlying principle remains: if a country’s own economic needs justify an exception, it should recognise that other countries have legitimate economic needs too. The arrangement also exposes the limits of sanctions as a foreign policy instrument. Sanctions can impose costs, but their effectiveness depends on consistency, international cooperation and credible enforcement. If restrictions are relaxed whenever the political price becomes too high, other countries may reasonably question whether the policy is based on principle or convenience. For India, this is an opportunity to make its case firmly without turning the issue into an unnecessary confrontation with Washington. India’s relationship with the United States is important across trade, technology, defence, education and the wider Indo-Pacific. New Delhi has no interest in allowing a disagreement over oil to damage cooperation in these areas and in no way, directly or indirectly, criticise it. However, a strong India-US partnership does not require India to accept every American demand. Strategic autonomy means maintaining the ability to make independent decisions while cooperating with other countries wherever interests converge. India should explain that its energy policy is neither directed against the United States nor intended to support any particular power. It is designed to ensure affordable and reliable supplies for a country of more than a billion people. New Delhi equally needs to remain conscious of the practical risks. We all understand that US sanctions and tariff measures can affect Indian exporters, banks, shipping companies and refiners. The answer is not to ignore these consequences, but to negotiate firmly, diversify energy sources and reduce excessive dependence on any single supplier. India should also continue investing in renewable energy, strategic petroleum reserves and long-term supply arrangements. These steps would provide greater protection against geopolitical shocks and reduce the ability of external powers to exert pressure through energy markets. The Russian diesel arrangement is unlikely, by itself, to resolve the global energy crisis. Supply disruptions linked to the West Asia, uncertainty around shipping routes and damage to energy infrastructure will continue to influence prices. But the episode offers India a clear diplomatic argument: what is good enough for America’s energy security cannot automatically be considered wrong for India’s. Washington has every right to pursue its national interests. India has the same right. The United States may use its laws to regulate transactions and impose sanctions, but it cannot reasonably expect India to treat American preferences as binding instructions in its foreign policy. IN the present century, data matters. New Delhi should make this point calmly, friendly, backed by facts and a clear assessment of its economic interests. It should avoid unnecessary rhetoric, but it should not surrender its decision-making space either. Finally, as is happening, New Delhi’s foreign policy must be guided by Indian interests. Partnerships with major powers are valuable, but they remain partnerships only when both sides recognise each other’s sovereignty. Trump’s Russian diesel deal has made that principle more relevant than ever.

opening: INDIA Bloc Marches to Supreme Court to File Plea Against CEC Gyanesh Kumar.
India’s democracy is facing a moment that demands constitutional introspection.
body: The Opposition’s campaign against alleged “vote chori” has acquired wider significance as sections of Gen Z join the call for electoral accountability and the Supreme Court intervenes to protect peaceful protest and ordinary public movement.

The convergence raises a question that cannot be answered merely through political rhetoric, police barricades or restrictions: can citizens trust the institutions responsible for safeguarding their democratic rights?
Democracy derives legitimacy not simply from announced results, but from public confidence in the fairness of the process.
“Vote Chori”: Allegations.
That Require Answers “Vote chori” expresses a basic concern: can every eligible Indian vote, and can the public trust the process?
Controversy surrounding the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls has intensified these questions.
Opposition parties have raised concerns about deletions, verification procedures and the Election Commission’s handling of objections.
The Commission has defended revision as necessary to maintain accurate rolls, citing deaths, migration and duplicate entries.
Allegations of deliberate manipulation must be tested through evidence, not treated as conclusively established.
The issue cannot be dismissed because political parties have raised it.
Electoral rolls are the foundation of representative democracy, and wrongful deletion can deprive an eligible voter of meaningful participation.
The answer lies in transparent procedures, accessible corrections and independent scrutiny.
Every disputed deletion should be explained and reviewed; credible evidence of irregularity should prompt investigation.
The Election Commission’s independence is a public trust that must be sustained through transparent and fair conduct.
Opposition and Gen Z: A Convergence Beyond Party Politics.
The protests reveal a new political convergence.
The Opposition’s credibility depends on evidence, consistency and a willingness to pursue constitutional remedies.
Young people’s participation adds another dimension.
Gen Z has grown up with digital access and expects institutions to explain decisions, justify restrictions and respond to scrutiny.
This convergence should neither be romanticised nor dismissed.
Allegations require evidence, protests must remain peaceful, and public authorities retain the duty to maintain law and order.
Criticism is not disloyalty, and dissent is not necessarily disorder.
Electoral concerns call for engagement, verification and redress—not an assumption that questioners must be silenced.
The Supreme Court’s Intervention.
The events surrounding protests in Delhi have raised a separate constitutional concern: how the State responds to peaceful dissent.
On October 11, 2026, a special Supreme Court bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana addressed restrictions affecting protesters and public movement.

The Court directed authorities to remove barricades that were not strictly warranted, ensure normal functioning of Metro and railway services, and prevent the unlawful detention of peaceful, unarmed protesters.
These directions reaffirm familiar constitutional principles.
The State may regulate assemblies and prevent violence, but restrictions must be lawful, pursue a legitimate objective and remain proportionate.
A capital city cannot be turned into a zone of indiscriminate restriction merely because a demonstration is politically inconvenient.
Disruptions to transport and limits on public assembly require justification grounded in law and necessity.
Article 19 protects speech and peaceful assembly, subject to lawful restrictions; Articles 21 and 14 protect liberty and guard against arbitrary State action.
These guarantees do not disappear when a government faces criticism.
The Court’s intervention places the balance between public order and civil liberty under judicial scrutiny.
Judicial Directions Are Not Optional.
The most serious concern arises from allegations that restrictions continued, or were implemented in ways inconsistent with the Court’s directions, despite judicial intervention.
Claims of police excess and unlawful detention require fair examination; deliberate disobedience must be established judicially.
The principle is clear: executive authorities cannot treat binding judicial directions as optional.
If clarification is needed, they should seek it; they cannot substitute their preferences for a court’s order.
Deliberate non-compliance, if established, would undermine judicial authority and public confidence; accountability must follow through lawful proceedings.
Police must facilitate lawful activity, prevent violence and protect citizens.
Force, detention and preventive restrictions must be justified by law and circumstances.
Peaceful protesters cannot be treated as offenders merely because their message embarrasses those in power.
Democracy Is More Than Winning Elections.
An elected government has a mandate to govern, not disregard constitutional limits.
Equally, an Opposition cannot treat every defeat as proof of manipulation.
The Election Commission should explain revision procedures, protect personal data while publishing relevant information, provide hearings to affected voters and address documented discrepancies.
Political parties and civil society should present verifiable evidence.
The judiciary must remain independent and impartial.
The government must show its confidence in democracy by accepting scrutiny, while Parliament should consider strengthening safeguards for voter registration.
The Constitutional Test.
The Opposition–Gen Z convergence is a reminder that public trust must be earned, not commanded.
The government can answer allegations with facts and restore institutional confidence.
It should not mistake the management of public order for the suppression of public opinion.
A strong government is not one that prevents uncomfortable questions, but one that answers them convincingly.
The Court has reiterated that constitutional government is defined by restraint as well as authority.
Alleged irregularities and violations of judicial orders must be determined through evidence and due process.
Neither slogans nor official denials can substitute for a credible examination of the facts.
India’s democratic strength lies in its Constitution, independent institutions and citizens’ freedom to question those who govern them.
“Vote chori” must ultimately be tested through evidence and accountability, but the slogan must not become an excuse to avoid scrutiny.
The ballot belongs to the citizen; the Constitution binds the government; the judiciary safeguards the limits of State power; and peaceful dissent remains essential to democratic life.
The real test of democracy is not whether those in power can silence their critics, but whether they can command public confidence while allowing their conduct to be questioned.
That is the constitutional challenge before India today.

stories.title: SKUAST-K’s Green Campus Roadmap
stories.summary: Climate change is no longer a far-off environmental concern confined to scientific discussions and policy documents. The Himalayan region of Kashmir stands at the centre of this emerging climate challenge. Extreme weather events have further intensified these problems. The devastating floods of 2014, which affected nearly 2.5 million people, claimed more than 280 lives, and caused estimated economic losses of around ₹1 lakh crore, remind us of Kashmir’s vulnerability to climate extremes. The unpredictability continues during 2026; J&K witnessed a marked increase in extreme rainfall events. According to the Director of the Meteorological Center, Kashmir, DrMukhtar Ahmad, 44 cloudbursts have struck Jammu and Kashmir since the onset of the monsoon this year, claiming about 35lives. These cloudburst incidents further triggered flash floods in Districts including Shopian, Anantnag, Bandipora and Budgam. The events have caused extensive damage to roads, bridges, homes and agricultural land, underscoring the region’s increasing vulnerability to climate-induced weather vagaries and the growing frequency of high-impact rainfall events. Universities as Climate Solution Hubs For a region where agriculture, horticulture, livestock, and natural resources sustain millions of livelihoods, climate resilience is now a necessity. In this backdrop, the Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology of Kashmir (SKUAST-K) has developed and adopted its Green and Sustainable Campuses Policy, marking a paradigm shift from a conventional campus to a climate-smart institution. This Policy brings together the seven vast campuses, all research stations, and KrishiVigyanKendras (KVKs) to create a vibrant ecosystem that works towards resource-efficient, climate-smart, and low-carbon spaces, aligning itself with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Restoring Landscapes One of the major policy initiatives of SKUAST-K is its focus on restoring and reclaiming degraded landscapes and wastelands. The University has, on a massive scale, undertaken plantation, landscaping, and biodiversity enhancement initiatives across its campuses. Through cleaning drives, landscape development, and ecological rehabilitation, the neglected and degraded areas within university campuses have been systematically restored. The development of lawns, gardens, roadside landscapes, biodiversity spaces, and green recreational areas has transformed previously underutilized spaces into productive ecological assets. At its main campus in Shalimar, approximately 22,000 square feet of area has been converted into green lawn cover, along with the planting of 1,800 saplings of diverse species. These interventions have enhanced campus aesthetics and beautification besides aiding carbon sequestration, biodiversity enrichment, and improved microclimatic conditions. article_sentences: New Delhi: The Supreme Court on Monday clarified that it had not adjudicated on the Election Commission of India's (ECI) modified Form 6 declaration for new voter registration, observing that the revised form was not before it when it decided the Bihar Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls case.

A bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana made the clarification while hearing a fresh petition raising concerns over the functioning of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and the changes to Form 6, which requires applicants seeking registration as new voters to disclose whether they or their parents were mapped in the previous SIR.

During the hearing, counsel for the petitioner submitted that the Supreme Court had clarified on October 5 that the modified Form 6 had not been approved by it, while the ECI had claimed that the revised declaration had received the top court's approval.

Responding to the submission, Justice Bagchi said the Supreme Court had not adjudicated on the new Form 6, adding that the revised form was not in existence when the judgment in the Bihar SIR case was delivered.
"There is no adjudication on the new Form 6," he observed, clarifying that the apex court's earlier oral remarks could not be construed as either approving or disapproving the modified declaration.
CJI Surya Kant cautioned against selectively interpreting the top court's observations for media reports, saying: "Please don't pick words for news items."

The clarification comes amid a political row over the modified Form 6 declaration, with questions being raised about the circumstances in which the changes were introduced and whether they were implemented despite objections from two Election Commissioners.

The controversy intensified after the ECI issued a press release on September 26 suggesting that the Supreme Court had upheld the revised declaration in its May 2026 judgment concerning the Bihar SIR exercise.
However, the modified declaration was introduced after the judgment, and the Supreme Court had no occasion to examine its contents while deciding the Bihar SIR matter.
Under the revised declaration, applicants seeking registration as new voters are required to state whether they or their parents were included in the previous SIR.
The earlier version of Form 6 used during the SIR exercise in other states did not contain this requirement.

The changes have also triggered allegations concerning the decision-making process within the ECI, with objections reportedly raised by two election commissioners on the ground that the declaration could not be modified without an amendment to the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, by the Central government.

stories.title: Dignity of asking questions restored
stories.summary: Frankly speaking, I am not going to assess the performance of the Omar Abdullah government over the past two years. It is quite unfair to judge a government that is not even half as empowered as the governments I have seen since late 1970s. A government in Jammu and Kashmir was never a complete one, because it was always sought to be guided by forces other than those elected to govern. This has been true since the times of Sheikh Abdullah, even when he was regarded as the supreme leader and the state enjoyed the full autonomy that his descendants are yearning for today. Had the governments in J&K been given the authority to govern, Sheikh Abdullah would not have been deposed in 1953. Historians have the right to ask: if his government was dismissed for harbouring secessionist thoughts, why was he brought back to power? Congress owes this answer to the nation. Fast forward this to 2026: as Omar Abdullah the first Chief Minister of the Union Territory is about to complete two years in office in a couple of days, the complexities have multiplied. Today is the time to analyze things since October 8, 2024—the day the results of the Assembly polls made it clear that the National Conference, along with its allies, had won a majority of seats. Yet, it took eight days for his swearing-in ceremony. This is a rare period in the history of Jammu and Kashmir—not just because there are two overlapping centers of authority ordained by the UT status, but because of the kind of political, social, and cultural narratives it has engendered. It felt like a civilizational rebirth in Kashmir when people saw a reflection of their urges and aspirations in the government they voted to power. Notwithstanding the election results and the hyperbolic greetings offered to democracy in Jammu and Kashmir, the elected National Conference-Congress government has had to contend with an entrenched perception that the Abdullahs’ party represents a Kashmir-oriented political project. A lot of commentary, containing some very fair points, has been written and spoken by the opposition parties—the BJP in particular, though local opposition groups have been equally critical and harsh—in assessing the government’s performance and declaring it unsuccessful in delivering on its manifesto promises. The opposition has an inherent right in a democratic setup to assess and reassess the performance of the government, but the repeated questioning of the mandate itself goes against the established norms of a functioning democracy. The opposition could not have ignored the issues that concern the people. They challenged the government on everything from electricity supply to the regularization of daily wagers and jobs for the jobless.
